program_overview.title: German Informatics Competitions: Biber, BwInf and BWKI
program_overview.tagline: From Biber puzzles to Bundeswettbewerb algorithms and an AI project for the BWKI, live and in English, with a mentor who matches your pace and accent.
program_overview.description:
This is a live online course for pupils in Germany, roughly ages 9 to 19, who want to take part in the German informatics competitions and do well in them. It runs from computational thinking puzzles for the Informatik-Biber, through programming tasks for the Jugendwettbewerb Informatik, to algorithmic problems for the Bundeswettbewerb Informatik, plus a machine-learning project track for the Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz (BWKI).

Classes are live and taught in English only. The mentor matches each pupil's pace and accent: speaks clearly, slows down, rephrases and checks understanding. A pupil whose first language is German gets competition training and English practice in the same class, and English fits this field well: code is written in English words, and the BWKI accepts projects in German or English ("Projekte dürfen sowohl auf deutscher wie auch auf englischer Sprache abgegeben werden"). We never teach in German.

The competitions form a ladder, all run by their organisers, not by us. BWINF calls the Informatik-Biber "Deutschlands größter Schülerwettbewerb im Bereich Informatik": a free online quiz for Jahrgangsstufen 3 to 13 that takes 30 to 40 minutes, and the 2026 Biber weeks run from 9 to 20 November 2026. The Jugendwettbewerb Informatik is open from Jahrgangsstufe 3, with a new level system from 2026 (Bronze for Klasse 5 and 6, Silber for 7 to 9, Gold from 10), and its 2026 round 3, using the two junior tasks of the Bundeswettbewerb, closes on 23 November 2026. The 45th Bundeswettbewerb Informatik, for young people up to 21 not yet studying or working, runs round 1 from 1 September to 23 November 2026, round 2 from early 2027 to April 2027 and round 3 in September 2027; BWINF says round 2 can count as the besondere Lernleistung in the Abitur, depending on Land and school. The BWKI, run by the Tübingen AI Center for Sekundarstufe I and II pupils, asks for a machine-learning project with written documentation, runnable code and a video pitch.

At the top of the ladder is the International Olympiad in Informatics. BWINF says the 39th IOI takes place from 12 to 19 September 2027 at the Hasso-Plattner-Institut in Potsdam, the second time Germany has hosted after 1992, and that the German team is chosen from up to 20 of the strongest participants in the Bundeswettbewerb. Every puzzle, task and mock contest in this course is our own, written in each competition's style; we never reproduce real competition tasks. We are independent of BWINF, the Tübingen AI Center and every organiser, we are not an official partner of any competition, and entries are made through the organisers' own sites, never through us.
what_makes_this_different: Live classes in English only, with a mentor who matches your pace and accent: useful practice for a field where code, papers and the BWKI pitch can all be in English
One ladder from age 9 to 19: Biber puzzles, Jugendwettbewerb tasks, Bundeswettbewerb algorithms and a BWKI machine-learning project
Batches by level, so a Klasse 4 puzzle solver and a Klasse 12 algorithm student never share a pace
Written solutions trained as hard as code, because the Bundeswettbewerb asks for explained solutions, not just programs
A BWKI project track covering data, model, evaluation, documentation, runnable code and a two to four minute video pitch
Original puzzles and contest tasks only, and honest about what we are: independent, not an official partner of any competition

learning_path.phase_1: Computational thinking for the Informatik-Biber and Jugendwettbewerb Bronze: logic, encoding, graphs, sorting and first programming tasks
learning_path.phase_2: Algorithms for Jugendwettbewerb Silber and Gold and Bundeswettbewerb round 1: simulation, search, greedy methods, recursion, graphs and dynamic programming, with written solutions
learning_path.phase_3: Bundeswettbewerb round 2 depth with running time and an introduction to C++, plus a BWKI machine-learning project from idea to video pitch

career_outcomes: Confident, calm performance in timed puzzle and programming contests
Algorithmic thinking: modelling a problem and choosing a method
Clear written solutions that explain an idea and prove it works
A real machine-learning project with documentation and a pitch
Python skill, and a first step into C++ for olympiad-level training
Technical English for papers, documentation and presentations

phase_1_computational_thinking.title: PHASE 1: Computational Thinking for the Biber and Jugendwettbewerb (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_computational_thinking.description: The puzzle level: informatics ideas without heavy coding, then the first short programming tasks. Older pupils move through this phase faster.

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: The Competition Ladder and Logic Puzzles
topics: A diagnostic puzzle set of our own to place each pupil at the right level
How we work in English: the mentor's pace, phrases for asking to repeat, and a German to English puzzle-word list
The competition ladder: Biber, Jugendwettbewerb, Bundeswettbewerb, BWKI and the IOI, with 2026 and 2027 dates
The Biber format: 9 tasks in 30 minutes at primary level, 12 in 35 minutes for Klasse 5 and 6, 15 in 40 minutes from Klasse 7
Logic puzzles: if-then rules, truth and elimination
Reading a puzzle carefully in English and restating it in your own words
projects: A personal puzzle journal with every solved task explained in one sentence
week_1_2.practice: Timed sets of our own Biber-style puzzles, then a class review

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Encoding, Graphs and Sorting Ideas
topics: Encoding information: binary, simple codes and error detection
Graphs as dots and lines: paths, networks and shortest routes by hand
Sorting and ordering puzzles, and comparing strategies
Trees and decision diagrams
Patterns and rules in sequences of symbols
Explaining a solution strategy out loud in English
projects: A puzzle of the pupil's own invention, solved by the batch
week_3_4.practice: Mixed puzzle sets of our own under time
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: a timed mock in the Biber style, our own tasks

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: Programs as Instructions
topics: Giving precise instructions to a robot or turtle on a grid
Sequences, loops and conditions in Python (or blocks for younger pupils)
Variables and counting
Finding the shortest program that solves a task
Tracing a program by hand to predict what it does
Bronze level practice: short tasks under time
projects: A grid robot that collects items and avoids walls, written in Python
week_5_6.practice: Our own short programming tasks in the Jugendwettbewerb style

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Loops, Lists and Simple Simulations
topics: Lists of values and looping through them
Simulating a process step by step
Counting and searching in a list
Debugging under time pressure
Silber level preview: tasks with more steps
Reviewing a solved task in English
projects: A simulation of a queue at a school canteen
week_7_8.practice: Timed sets of our own programming tasks
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a timed mock of original puzzles and programming tasks

phase_2_algorithms.title: PHASE 2: Algorithms for the Jugendwettbewerb and Bundeswettbewerb Round 1 (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_algorithms.description: The algorithm level, in Python: classic methods, written solutions and the habit of testing on tricky inputs.

month_3_search_greedy_recursion.title: Month 3: Search, Greedy Methods and Recursion

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Brute Force, Simulation and Greedy Methods
topics: Modelling a problem: what is the input, what is the output
Brute force: trying all options, and when that is fast enough
Greedy methods: when choosing the best step now works, and a counterexample when it does not
Sorting as a tool for solving other problems
Testing with small cases, edge cases and large cases
Gold level practice: longer tasks with several parts
projects: A scheduling solver with a greedy method and a test set
week_9_10.practice: Our own algorithm tasks with written explanations

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Recursion and Backtracking
topics: Recursion: base case and recursive case
Backtracking: exploring choices and undoing them
Permutations, subsets and puzzle solvers
Pruning to make a search faster
Counting how many steps an algorithm takes
Writing a short, clear explanation of why a method is correct
projects: A Sudoku or tiling solver using backtracking
week_11_12.practice: Timed algorithm sets of our own
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a timed contest of our own tasks

month_4_graphs_dp_writeups.title: Month 4: Graphs, Dynamic Programming and Written Solutions

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Graph Algorithms
topics: Graphs in code: adjacency lists and matrices
Breadth-first search and depth-first search
Shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm
Connected components and cycles
Grids as graphs: mazes and flood fill
Choosing a graph model for a story problem
projects: A route planner for a small city map of our own
week_13_14.practice: Our own graph problems, coded and explained

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Dynamic Programming and the Written Submission
topics: Dynamic programming: storing answers to subproblems
Classic patterns: counting paths, knapsack and longest subsequences
Writing up a solution: the idea, the implementation, example runs and the source code
Group work in round 1 and individual work in round 2, as BWINF's rules set out
Planning a long contest: which task first, and when to stop
Presenting a solution to the batch in English
projects: A full written solution of our own Bundeswettbewerb-style task, with code and examples
week_15_16.practice: A take-home task of our own with a written write-up
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a timed contest plus a written solution, all original tasks

phase_3_round_two_and_bwki.title: PHASE 3: Bundeswettbewerb Round 2 Depth and a BWKI Project (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_round_two_and_bwki.description: Two tracks to choose from: contest depth toward round 2 and olympiad-style training, or a machine-learning project for the BWKI. Many pupils do both.

month_5_contest_depth.title: Month 5: Running Time, Harder Problems and C++

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Running Time and Efficient Algorithms
topics: O notation and estimating whether a solution is fast enough
Binary search on the answer
Prefix sums and two pointers
Priority queues and heaps
Harder dynamic programming and graph problems
Arguing correctness in a written solution
projects: A solution improved from slow to fast, with timings and an explanation
week_17_18.practice: Our own round 2 style problems with full write-ups

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: A First Step into C++ and Olympiad Context
topics: Why olympiad training uses C++: BWINF says IOI pre-selection training is programmed in C++
C++ basics for Python programmers: types, vectors and input and output
Rewriting a solved Python task in C++
The IOI path: the German team is chosen from up to 20 of the strongest participants in the Bundeswettbewerb over three training camps
IOI 2027 in Potsdam as context, and the 45th Bundeswettbewerb as the entry to selection for IOI 2028
Building a personal training plan
projects: Three of your own earlier solutions rewritten in C++
week_19_20.practice: Timed mixed contests of our own in Python or C++
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a timed contest of original problems

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: From Idea to Model
topics: What the BWKI asks for: a project that uses machine-learning methods, solo or in teams of up to four
Finding a question worth answering with data, and checking it is ethical
Collecting and cleaning a data set
Training a first model in Python, and splitting data for honest testing
Measuring accuracy and finding where the model fails
Keeping a project log in English
projects: A working first model with a test report
week_21_22.practice: Weekly project milestones reviewed in class

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Documentation, Code and the Video Pitch
topics: Improving the model and explaining every choice
Written documentation: question, data, method, results and limits
Runnable, readable code that someone else can run
A two to four minute video pitch, practised in English
Final contest-track review for pupils on that track
A plan for the next competition season
projects: A complete BWKI-style project: documentation, runnable code and a video pitch
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: a timed contest of original tasks or a project presentation, by track

faqs.question: What does this course prepare for?
faqs.answer: The German informatics competitions: the Informatik-Biber, the Jugendwettbewerb Informatik, the Bundeswettbewerb Informatik and the Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz (BWKI). It is a live online course for pupils in Germany aged roughly 9 to 19, taught in English, with batches by level.

faqs.question: Are the classes in German or in English?
faqs.answer: English only. We never teach in German. The mentor matches your pace and accent: speaks clearly, slows down, rephrases and checks understanding. Many families see this as a plus: competition training and English practice at once. Code uses English words anyway, and the BWKI accepts projects in German or English.

faqs.question: When is the Informatik-Biber 2026?
faqs.answer: BWINF says the 2026 Biber weeks run from 9 to 20 November 2026. Results follow in December 2026, and certificates and prizes are sent in January 2027. The Biber is free, for Jahrgangsstufen 3 to 13, and takes 30 to 40 minutes.

faqs.question: What are the Bundeswettbewerb Informatik dates?
faqs.answer: For the 45th Bundeswettbewerb, BWINF lists round 1 from 1 September to 23 November 2026, round 2 from early 2027 to April 2027 and round 3 in September 2027. Group work is allowed in round 1, and round 2 must be individual work.

faqs.question: What is the Jugendwettbewerb Informatik level system?
faqs.answer: From 2026 BWINF uses three levels: Bronze, recommended for Klasse 5 and 6, with 3 tasks in 30 minutes; Silber for Klasse 7 to 9, with 4 tasks in 40 minutes; and Gold from Klasse 10, with 6 tasks in 60 minutes. Participation is possible from Jahrgangsstufe 3. The 2026 round 3 closes on 23 November 2026.

faqs.question: What is the BWKI?
faqs.answer: The Bundeswettbewerb Künstliche Intelligenz, run by the Tübingen AI Center for pupils in Sekundarstufe I and II, solo or in teams of up to four. Projects must use machine-learning methods and include written documentation, runnable code and a video pitch. In 2026 the project deadline was 20 September 2026 and the final in Tübingen is on 13 November 2026; dates for the next round appear on the BWKI site.

faqs.question: What is the connection to IOI 2027 in Potsdam?
faqs.answer: BWINF says the 39th International Olympiad in Informatics takes place from 12 to 19 September 2027 at the Hasso-Plattner-Institut in Potsdam, and that the German team is chosen from up to 20 of the strongest participants in the Bundeswettbewerb over three training camps. The 45th Bundeswettbewerb, which started on 1 September 2026, is the entry to selection for IOI 2028 in Japan. We teach toward that path; we play no part in selection.

faqs.question: Are you an official partner of BWINF or the BWKI?
faqs.answer: No. We are an independent online school with teachers in India. We are not an official partner of any competition, and entries are made through the organisers' own sites, never through us. Every puzzle and task in this course is our own, written in the competitions' style.

faqs.question: My child is 9. Is that too young?
faqs.answer: No. The Biber and the Jugendwettbewerb are open from Jahrgangsstufe 3, and our puzzle level needs no coding. Batches are by level, so younger pupils work at their own pace.

faqs.question: Do you promise a prize or a place in round 2?
faqs.answer: No. We promise careful teaching, honest feedback and lots of practice. Results depend on the pupil and the competition.

faqs.question: When are classes, with the time difference to India?
faqs.answer: Timing is flexible on weekdays or weekends: choose a batch, or 1-on-1 at your convenience. Our teachers work in India time, which is 4 hours 30 minutes ahead of Germany in winter and 3 hours 30 minutes ahead in summer, so German afternoon, early evening and weekend slots are realistic.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first class is a free demo, so the pupil can meet the mentor, hear the pace and decide with no pressure.
